message.reasoning: The user wants to set a timer for 10 seconds using the timeout command. They say "You should use timeout 10." They likely want to run a command that waits 10 seconds. On Windows, the timeout command is used like "timeout /t 10". But they say "timeout 10". That might be Linux? In Linux, "timeout 10" would run a command for 10 seconds? Actually "timeout" in Linux is used as "timeout DURATION COMMAND". So "timeout 10" alone would not do anything. But maybe they want to run "timeout 10" which will wait 10 seconds and then exit. In Windows, "timeout /t 10" will wait 10 seconds. But they specifically say "timeout 10". That might be a Linux command: "timeout 10" will wait 10 seconds and then exit. But "timeout" expects a command to run. If no command, it will just wait? Actually "timeout" in GNU coreutils: "timeout DURATION COMMAND [ARG]..." So if no command, it will error. But maybe they want to run "timeout 10" to wait 10 seconds. Let's assume they want to run "timeout 10" on Linux. We can use the function to execute the command. We'll call the function with command "timeout 10". The unit can be "seconds". Let's do that.
